en: Title: *Saṃvarodaya*, Chapter 27 Author: Scriptural Source: TUL Matsunami no. 404, folio 79 recto 5–[end]
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme method for extracting the mantra:
on a delightful plot of ground smeared with scented water.
In a well-concealed and secluded place, provided with flowers and incense,
the mantra-practitioner, having caused [the vessel] to move, should then cause [the disciple] to consume the nectar.
Through union with his own tutelary deity, preceded by the offering of the bali-oblation,
the preceptor, being well-composed, [performs] the assembly of all ḍākinīs.
A beautiful triangular maṇḍala, with three lines encircling it on the outside,
[is situated] in the great garden of Dharmodayā, resplendent with various flowers.
There, one should write eight groups in sequence according to the division of vowels (ali) and consonants (kāli):
[the numbers] corresponding to Kāma, Rudra, Randhra, Muni, Bāṇa, and Agni.
Having laid out a grid of forty-nine squares according to the instruction, one begins with the letter *ā* and ends with the syllable *ha*.
O Lord of the Guhyakas, having understood this through the application of circumambulation, [one attains success].

Taking the fifth [letter] of the first square, one should place it above that very [position] with the thirteenth square. Adorned above with a dot by the third of the nine squares; the fifth of the seven squares should be taken, beautified below by the seed-syllable of fire (Ra). Adorned by the fourth of the first [square], O excellent beloved; the second syllable of the seventh [square] should be taken. The first of the eleventh square should be taken, and taking the fifth of the ninth square, it is beautified below by the letter Ja. The fourth of the seven squares should be taken; the eleventh of the first square, this being adorned on the head. Taking the fifth of the ninth square, it is beautified below by the fifth of the first. Taking the fifth of the fifth square; the fourth of the seven squares should be taken, beautified below by the fifth of the thirteenth square. It should be pronounced twice. Adorned above with a dot by the third of the ninth square; taking the second of the fifth square, it is joined with the fourth of the eleventh square. One should always mutter the Heart-mantra, which is the abode of all powers of accomplishment.

Taking the four-syllable [mantra] from the seventh square, it is split below by the fifth syllable of the ninth square. It is adorned with the fourth syllable of the first [square]. On both sides of the seventh [syllable] of the seventh [square], there are two dots (*bindu*). One should take the fourth syllable of the seventh square and recite it twice. Again, taking that same syllable, it is adorned below with the fifth vowel. One should recite twice the third syllable of the ninth square, adorned with a dot (*bindu*). One should take the second syllable of the fifth square; having taken the fourth syllable of the eleventh square, one should place the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) before the preceding word. Constantly and perpetually chanting this, it is the cause for achieving good fortune and spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).

Take the second syllable of the entire [first] square; the first syllable of the eleventh [square], adorned below by the son of Vahni (Ra); take the second syllable of the seventh [square], adorned by the twelfth [square] (Sa). Take the fifth syllable of the ninth square, adorned by the thirteenth [square] (Ma). Having taken the first syllable of the seventh [square], it is the supreme state (Parama-pada). Take the fourth syllable of the fifth square, adorned with the fourth vowel (Ī). Take the fourth syllable of the ninth square, adorned with the eleventh vowel (Ū). Take the fourth syllable of the seventh [square], adorned below with the fifth vowel (U), and likewise its head adorned with the third [vowel] (I) of the ninth [square]. That syllable which bestows liberation should be pronounced twice. Take the second syllable of the fifth [square]; the eleventh square joined with the fourth [vowel] (E). Take the second syllable of the seventh square, adorned below with the seventh syllable of the ninth square (Na), and adorned with the second vowel (Ā). One should take the fourth syllable of the seventh square, adorned with the second vowel (Ā). One should provide the first [syllable] with the prefix (Pra). One should cause this to be recited and meditated upon daily as the delight of the heart of the Yoginīs, bestowing the boon of all accomplishments.

Oṃ. One should first take the third letter of the seventh [row], adorned with the fifth vowel. Then, taking the second letter from the ninth square, one should adorn it with the third [vowel] as its head. Taking the fourth letter of the fifth square, it is adorned with the third vowel. Taking the third letter of the seventh square, it is beautified by the fifth vowel. One should take the second letter of the ninth square; there, it is adorned with the third [vowel]. Taking the fourth letter of the seventh square, it is joined with the fifth vowel. It is adorned with a *bindu* by means of the third letter of the ninth. There, the sequence is a double utterance. Taking the second letter of the fifth square, one should join it with the fourth letter of the eleventh square for the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Taking the letter of the first square, it is joined with the seventh vowel. Taking the fourth letter of the seventh square, it is joined with the fourth of the fifth square—this is auspicious. Then follows a word of double utterance. Taking the fourth letter of the seventh square, it is joined below with the fifth vowel, adorned with a half-moon and a *bindu*; then follows a word of double utterance. Taking the second letter of the fifth square, one should join it with the fourth of the eleventh square; this bestows supreme bliss. Having established it preceded by the *praṇava*, one should accomplish the supreme syllable by taking the letter of the single square and joining it with the seventh vowel. Taking the fourth of the seventh square, it is joined with the fourth of the fifth square and adorned with the second vowel. Taking the second of the third square, taking the second of the ninth square, taking the fourth of the ninth square, and taking the fourth of the ninth square again—this is a supreme word of double utterance. Taking the fourth letter of the seventh square, it is joined with the fifth vowel and adorned with a half-moon and a *bindu*. As for the word of double utterance: taking the second letter of the fifth square, it is joined with the fourth of the eleventh square for the Supreme Lord. Having first joined the *praṇava*, one should accomplish the supreme syllable.

Taking the first vowel of the thirteenth square, it is joined with the second vowel. Taking the fourth syllable of the fifth square, one should establish the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*). One should take the fourth syllable of the ninth square; it belongs to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Taking the fourth syllable of the seventh square, it should be adorned on its head by the thirteenth vowel. A wise person should place two dots (*bindu*) on the side of the seventh [syllable] using the seventh [vowel]. Taking the syllable from the second square of the seventh [group], it is adorned on its head by the third vowel. Taking the eighth syllable of the ninth square, one should bind it below with the fourth [vowel] in that very place. Joined with the second vowel, it is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*). Taking the fifth syllable of the ninth square, it is beautified by the third vowel. Taking the first [syllable] of the eleventh square, when established, it bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). Taking the fourth syllable of the seventh square, it is joined with the fifth vowel and adorned with the half-moon and the dot (*ardhendubindu*). The Supreme Lord should be uttered twice. Taking the second syllable of the fifth [group], it is joined with the fourth of the eleventh square; this is the supreme state.
One should know the extraction of the mantra from the region of the Guru and the Fire; [for] by means of those mantras read from books alone, devoid of the oral tradition,
one shall not attain the state of accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of aeons.
When the tenth festival day has arrived, honored by Vajrayoginī,
with various kinds of flowers and accompanied by food and drink.
The mantra is indeed the form of the Yoginī, and the Yoginī is the form of the mantra;
one who desires the supreme state must not create a distinction between the two.
It is better to give up one's life than for life to be lost;
if one desires supreme accomplishment, one must then protect the samaya.
The entire universe, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, originates from the Left;
the yogi, always practicing the way of the Left, should step forward with the left foot first.
One should perform worship with the left hand, guarding the left palm;
one should practice the conduct of five colors while conceiving them as a single color.
Thus, one is liberated from all conceptual constructions and freed from all dualities.
The Guru is the Buddha, the Guru is the Dharma, and likewise the Guru is the Saṅgha;
therefore, one should propitiate the Guru with the desire for the state of Buddhahood.
The *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasamvara*.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the section on the procedure for extracting the mantras.
